brief: How to look at your own work without flinching or flattering it

slots.titleAccent: on the day you made it.
slots.subtitle: Six ways to judge work you are too close to, none of which involve waiting until you feel objective.
slots.plate1Body: Fresh work is indistinguishable from good work for about forty-eight hours.
slots.plate2Body: Change the conditions you look under, not how hard you look.
slots.coverNote: The last one is the reason the other five keep failing

slots.body: At full size you read the parts you laboured over. At a tenth of the size you see only the arrangement, which is the thing a stranger sees first and the thing you are least able to judge up close.
slots.plate1Body: If the shape stops working small, the detail was never the problem.
slots.plate2Body: Blur removes craft and leaves hierarchy. Hierarchy is what fails.
slots.plate3Body: Reading stops and looking starts, which is the whole trick.
slots.plate4Body: Not to feel bad. To see which decisions you never actually made.

slots.body: The attachment fades faster than the memory of the effort, which is why a gap of days is worth more than a gap of hours. You do not become more objective; you simply stop defending the parts that cost you something.
slots.plate1Body: One night removes most of the sunk cost you are protecting.
slots.plate2Body: Tired judgement is uniformly harsher and uniformly wrong.
slots.plate3Body: Half of what you were about to cut is fine.
slots.plate4Body: Distance improves judgement and does not improve the work.

slots.body: Liking is the least useful signal available and the first one you reach for. Every question that produces a decision is a question about somebody else, or about what the work is for.
slots.plate1Body: Answer in one sentence, or the review has nothing to measure against.
slots.plate2Body: Name the specific person and what specifically loses them.
slots.plate3Body: Forced removal finds what is load-bearing faster than praise does.
slots.plate4Body: The harder question, and the one nobody volunteers unprompted.

slots.body: Unbounded feedback returns whatever the reader noticed first, which is usually a colour. Naming what you want examined is not defensiveness; it is the difference between an opinion and a review.
slots.plate1Body: Rough edges you already know about, so nobody spends the round on them.
slots.plate2Body: More than one and you get the easiest answered, not the hardest.
slots.plate3Body: The explanation you give is the thing the work should have done.
slots.plate4Body: Argue with feedback tomorrow. Record it today.

slots.body: The hours went into the part nobody will look at, and you cannot stop yourself from weighting it. Nothing about the work communicates what it cost, which is a fact about all work and not a failure of this one.
slots.plate1Body: The hardest section is frequently the most disposable one.
slots.plate2Body: If the piece survives, it was decoration all along.
slots.plate3Body: Then find out which cleverness anybody actually missed.
slots.plate4Body: What was wrong here is often exactly right somewhere else.

slots.body: That gap is the whole difficulty, and it never closes — it is why the work looks worse to you each year while looking better to everybody else. There is no technique in this set that fixes it, because it is not a problem.
slots.plate1Body: Being able to see the flaw is what precedes being able to fix it.
slots.plate2Body: It widens with taste, which is what improving actually feels like.
slots.plate3Body: Waiting for work you are happy with means waiting permanently.
slots.plate4Body: This piece against the last one, not against the one in your head.

slots.eyebrow: On the thing you are avoiding sending
slots.body: Three of the six take an evening between them, and the piece you are protecting is almost certainly finished already.
slots.plate1Body: One night, and the version of you who wanted to keep polishing.
slots.plate2Body: The only feedback that has ever improved anything — somebody else's.
